title: Dust, airborne contaminants and exposure uncertainty
audience: Cleaners working in warehouses where dust of unknown origin or possible hazardous material is present.
learningOutcomes: Identify uncertain particulate sources and airborne visibility changes in a warehouse.
Explain why unidentified dust is never dry-swept, and why authorised supervision is needed.
Stop and refer a powder spill of unknown origin, leaving the area restricted.

instruction.heading: Where warehouse dust comes from
instruction.body: A warehouse can produce dust from many sources at once. Stored goods can shed fine material, and packaging, cardboard, pallets and dunnage (the timber or packing used to protect loads) generate fibres and fine particles. Bulk materials such as grains, minerals, plastics, fertilisers or powders can leave residues on floors, ledges and the tops of racking. Chemicals can leak, be spilled or be stored in damaged containers, and their residues can look like ordinary dust. The same ordinary-looking powder can be harmless in one place and a serious hazard in another, because its risk depends on what it is, how much there is, how it is spread into the air, and what is stored nearby. A cleaner cannot tell these apart by looking, and that is the core reason this lesson exists.

instruction.heading: Signs that a source is uncertain
instruction.body: Treat a particulate source as uncertain when you cannot say what it is from its label, its packaging or the site's records. Other warning signs include a visible haze in the air that was not there earlier, a change in the colour or texture of a residue, a sharp or unusual smell, a powder on surfaces with no matching stock nearby, a leaking or damaged container, and any report from a colleague of breathing or eye irritation. A report of irritation is a signal to stop the task and get the source checked, even if nobody feels unwell at the time. Do not disturb an unidentified residue in order to find out what it is. Disturbing it can put it into the air, and the act of checking then becomes the exposure.

instruction.heading: Why unknown dust is never dry-swept
instruction.body: Dry sweeping lifts fine material into the air, where it can be breathed in or settle onto other surfaces, equipment and food. The same action can also make dust cloud in a way that becomes a fire or explosion risk. State regulator guidance says that combustible dust can create a hazardous area when it is present in a suitable quantity and form, and that the person managing the workplace must manage hazardous atmospheres, including ignition sources. Do not use dry sweeping, compressed air or a leaf blower on unidentified dust. Wet methods and vacuums are not automatically safe either, because some materials react with water and standard vacuums are not designed for fine or hazardous dust. Any cleaning method for an unknown residue is chosen by the site authority and the specialist, and not by the cleaner.

instruction.heading: Stop conditions and the chemicals register
instruction.body: A powder spill of unknown origin near bulk chemical storage is a stop condition. Keep people out of the area, do not switch electrical equipment on or off in or beside the spill, and keep ignition sources away. Then check whether the site has a hazardous chemicals register. The register must list the hazardous chemicals used, handled or stored at the workplace, each entry must have a current safety data sheet (SDS), and the register must be easy for workers to reach. Model duties also require the supplier to provide the SDS with the chemical, and require the business to identify, assess and control risks and to store chemicals safely. If the site cannot match the powder to an entry, that is a finding to record, not a reason to guess. Never assume a powder is harmless because it looks like something on the register.

instruction.heading: Recording, referral and restriction
instruction.body: Your job is to make the condition safe to leave, record it accurately, and refer it. Write down the time, the exact location, the work-order number, and what you observed. Keep what you saw separate from what you think it might be, and label your guesses as guesses. Record the supporting evidence, such as a photograph taken from a safe distance if the site allows it, and the names of the people you told. Specialist identification and any sampling are arranged by the site and carried out by a qualified person. A cleaner does not take samples, does not identify the material, and does not decide that an area is clear. The restriction stays in place until a documented authority releases it, and a quick wipe by the cleaner does not end the restriction.

instruction.heading: Respiratory protection and symptoms
instruction.body: Respiratory protection is used only as the site's dust assessment requires, and only by workers who have been fitted and trained for it. A worker should not enter a restricted area because they are wearing a mask. Where the site requires a respirator, a fit check is done each time it is worn, and the choice of respirator is made by the site, not by the cleaner. If you or a colleague develop breathing trouble, skin or eye irritation, or any other symptom, stop, move to fresh air where it is safe to do so, and follow the site's first aid and emergency procedure. Report the symptoms to the supervisor and record them.

instruction.heading: The limits of this lesson
instruction.body: This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or fire-safety approval, and it does not authorise sampling, identification, clearance or entry into a restricted area. Completing it does not make a cleaner a specialist in hazardous materials, dust control or atmosphere testing.

procedure: Identify uncertain particulate sources: an unlabelled residue, a visible haze, a change in smell or texture, a leaking container, or a report of irritation.
Do not disturb the residue, and do not dry sweep, use compressed air or use a blower on it.
If the residue is near bulk chemical storage, treat it as a stop condition. Keep people out, avoid switching electrical equipment in or beside the spill, and keep ignition sources away.
Check the hazardous chemicals register for a matching entry and its SDS, and record what you found, including if no match exists.
Refer to the site authority and the qualified specialist for identification and any sampling. Do not sample or identify it yourself.
Record the observation, the inference labelled as an inference, the people notified, the restriction and the time.
Keep the area restricted until a documented authority releases it in writing.

workedExamples.situation: A powder spill of unknown origin appears near bulk chemical storage.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do first, and what do you refuse to do?
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop. Do not dry-sweep the powder or use compressed air. Keep people out of the area, avoid switching electrical equipment in or beside the spill, and record the location and time without disturbing the spill. Check the chemicals register for a matching entry, and report that no match was found if none exists. Refer to the site authority and leave the area restricted pending documented authority and specialist controls.

workedExamples.situation: During a routine clean, you notice a fine layer of material on the top of a pallet-racking beam that you can reach from the walkway. The packaging on the pallets below is labelled with a known product, and the site records show that product is stored in the same bay.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can you clean the layer with the usual dry method?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. A layer that matches a known product is still a combustible or nuisance dust risk, so the usual dry method is not appropriate. Do not sweep it up. Record the location and the matching product, tell the supervisor, and ask for the site's approved method for that product. Check the product's SDS through the register so the approved method is based on the right information. Do not work at height to reach the beam unless the site has authorised it.

workedExamples.situation: A colleague sweeping near a pallet of unlabelled drums reports eye irritation and a cough. The sweeping has been going on for about ten minutes.
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop the sweeping and do not continue. Move the colleague away from the area to fresh air where it is safe to do so, and follow the site's first aid and emergency procedure. Keep other people out of the area, report the symptoms and the drums to the supervisor at once, and record the times, the symptoms and who was told. Leave the drums and the residue undisturbed for the site authority to assess.

equipmentAndPpe: Respiratory protection only as the site's dust assessment requires, with a fit check each time it is worn.
Eye protection and gloves suitable for the material, as the site or the SDS requires.
Disposable coveralls where the site requires them for the residue.
Barrier tape, cones or signs to restrict the area.
Access to the hazardous chemicals register and the SDS for listed substances.
Record form for observations, referrals and restrictions.
Phone or radio to reach the supervisor and the site authority.

commonErrors.error: Dry-sweeping an unknown powder because it is only a little.
commonErrors.prevention: Never dry-sweep unidentified dust. Stop, keep clear, and refer.

commonErrors.error: Using compressed air or a blower to clear a residue from a rack or ledge.
commonErrors.prevention: Compressed air and blowers spread dust. Do not use them on unidentified residue.

commonErrors.error: Taking a sample or testing the powder to find out what it is.
commonErrors.prevention: Sampling and identification are done by a qualified person under the site authority.

commonErrors.error: Assuming a powder is harmless because it looks like flour, salt or dust from packaging.
commonErrors.prevention: Appearance does not show hazard. Check the register and the SDS, and refer the residue if no match exists.

commonErrors.error: Reopening the area after a quick wipe.
commonErrors.prevention: The restriction stays until a documented authority releases it in writing.

commonErrors.error: Switching lights, fans or equipment on or off beside a spill near chemicals.
commonErrors.prevention: Leave electrical equipment as it is and keep ignition sources away from the spill.

commonErrors.error: Recording a guess as an observation.
commonErrors.prevention: Write what you saw, and label anything you think it might be as an inference.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Model duties require a register of hazardous chemicals used, handled or stored at the workplace, with a current SDS for each listed chemical, kept where workers can readily reach it (Safe Work Australia, hazardous chemicals register page; no date shown; checked 2026-11-03). Check your state or territory regulator for any extra rules.

Model duties require the supplier to provide an SDS with a hazardous chemical, and require the business to identify, assess and control risks, store chemicals safely, and control ignition sources and any build-up of flammable substances (Safe Work Australia, WHS duties related to hazardous chemicals; the page shows only a 2011 model-law note as a date; checked 2026-11-03).

State regulator guidance (SafeWork NSW, hazardous atmospheres; last modified 2025-10-03) says combustible dust can create a hazardous area and that the workplace must manage hazardous atmospheres, including ignition sources. The guidance gives no dust-specific control measures, so site-specific controls must come from the authorised person.
Do not apply any of them from this lesson alone.

This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval or fire-safety approval, and it does not authorise sampling, identification or clearance. Completing it does not make a cleaner a specialist.

qualityStandard: In the simulated site plan, every uncertain particulate source is identified, with the reason it is uncertain.
In the case study, dry sweeping and compressed air are refused, with a stated reason.
The restriction and referral are recorded, and the observation is kept separate from the inference, with no claim that the area is clear.
documentationEvidence: Dust observation record with time, location, what was seen, and any inference labelled as an inference.
Chemicals register check record showing whether a matching entry and SDS exist, or that none was found.
Restriction and referral record with the authorising officer named, or recorded as not yet named.
summary: Treat dust of unknown origin as uncertain. Do not disturb it, and never dry-sweep it or use compressed air.
A powder spill near bulk chemicals is a stop condition: keep people out, keep ignition sources away, and refer.
Record what you saw, keep inference separate, and keep the area restricted until a documented authority releases it.

knowledgeChecks.question: A powder of unknown origin is near bulk chemicals. What is the correct action?
options: Dry-sweep it quickly, since it is only a small amount
Keep people out, record it without disturbing it, and refer
Take a sample yourself, then label it and keep it in the van

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must unknown dust not be dry-swept?
options: It makes the floor slippery for the crew and the visitors
The broom will break and the crew will need a new one
It lifts dust into the air, which may be hazardous

knowledgeChecks.question: How long should the area stay restricted?
options: Until documented authority and specialist controls are given
Until it looks clean to the eye and the area seems dry
Until lunch, when the supervisor is back on the site

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the first place to check whether a chemical on site is recorded?
options: A colleague's memory of the stock
A label on a bag you find nearby

knowledgeChecks.question: Which of these does the lesson list as a warning sign that a dust source is uncertain?
options: A visible haze in the air that was not there earlier
A labelled bag of known stock
